newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore change could cut political growth-analyst.
newsitem.headline: Singapore change could cut political growth-analyst.

text.p: Sweeping changes to Singapore's electoral laws could stunt its political growth by discouraging opposition candidates from running for office, political analysts said on Friday.
Singapore on Thursday announced plans to change electoral boundaries ahead of general elections due by April 1997, slashing the number of single-member seats from 21 to nine.

Except for five wards, the boundaries of other electoral divisions would be changed, said a report by the electoral boundaries review committee. Its recommendations are expected to be implemented ahead of general elections.

The changes were not surprising as parliament in October approved allowing each multi-member group representation constituency (GRC) to elect a maximum of six people, up from the current four, opposition figures said. But they called the decision unfair and said it would limit their election chances.
However, ruling party MPs said the new boundaries would foster stronger community ties as bigger GRCs allowed for better representation in town councils.
The government said the changes were aimed at shifting more authority and responsibility to local communities and their members of parliament (MPs).

While the number of GRCs is maintained at 15, the number of MPs to be chosen in them would rise to 74 from the current 60. The larger GRCs are expected to be anchored by senior members of the cabinet, analysts said.
"The whole concept of expanding the GRC may serve a short-term interest of ensuring that potential leaders are assured of being elected," political scientist Hussin Mutalib told Reuters.

"But the very fact that you have these expanded teams headed by the top guns...there is a high likelihood that the GRCs would not be contested because the opposition candidates must be thinking about losing their (election) deposits."
He said this does not augur well for Singapore's long term political development.

"Without a contest, you will deny and deprive the ruling regime of a useful barometer to measure the level of ground support because a no-contest may not necessarily mean full mandate and legitimacy for the government," he said.
National Solidarity Party President Tan Chee Kien told the Straits Times newspaper the ruling People's Action Party always changes the rules before the game starts.
"As usual, they are trying to protect their so-called talent under the political umbrella of GRCs and indirectly they show that these people cannot stand on their own two feet," he said.

But Walter Woon, a nominated member of parliament, said if the opposition was able to form a strong team, they now have the best chance to win four to six seats with one swoop. "If they blow it now, they blow it for the next decade."

He said the GRC system is "an excellent one because you can have no one-shot party like the Greens or a one-race party. It means you need to have a team, you need to have a policy (and) you need a multi-racial group."
